questions.question: A 5 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s². What is the net force acting on it?
questions.explanation: F = ma = 5 kg × 3 m/s² = 15 N. Always multiply mass by acceleration to find net force.

questions.question: A force of 24 N acts on a 6 kg object. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: a = F/m = 24 N ÷ 6 kg = 4 m/s². Rearrange F = ma to solve for acceleration.

questions.question: What is the momentum of a 3 kg ball moving at 8 m/s?
questions.explanation: p = mv = 3 kg × 8 m/s = 24 kg·m/s.

questions.question: A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 seconds. What is the net force?
A box of mass 8 kg is pushed with 40 N force. What is the acceleration?
The coefficient of kinetic friction between a surface and a 10 kg block is 0.3. What is the friction force? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Friction force f = μmg = 0.3 × 10 × 10 = 30 N. Normal force on a flat surface equals mg.

questions.question: A 4 kg object moving at 5 m/s collides and joins a stationary 6 kg object. What is the combined velocity after collision?
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum: m₁v₁ = (m₁+m₂)v₂ → 4×5 = (4+6)×v₂ → 20 = 10v₂ → v₂ = 2 m/s.

questions.question: A truck of mass 2000 kg travels at 15 m/s. What is its momentum?
A 50 N force decelerates a 10 kg object. What is the magnitude of deceleration?
questions.explanation: a = F/m = 50 ÷ 10 = 5 m/s². The deceleration magnitude is 5 m/s².

questions.question: An object starts from rest and reaches 30 m/s in 6 seconds. What is its acceleration?
A 15 kg box rests on a surface with μ = 0.4. What minimum force is needed to start it moving? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Static friction force = μmg = 0.4 × 15 × 10 = 60 N. The applied force must exceed this to start motion.

questions.question: If friction is removed from a surface, what happens to the minimum force needed to move an object?
questions.explanation: Friction is the only horizontal resistance on a flat surface. Without friction, any infinitesimally small force could theoretically accelerate the object.

questions.question: A 200 g ball (0.2 kg) is thrown at 15 m/s. What is its momentum?
questions.explanation: p = mv = 0.2 × 15 = 3 kg·m/s. Remember to convert grams to kilograms first.

questions.question: An object with momentum 60 kg·m/s decelerates to rest in 3 seconds. What is the braking force?
questions.explanation: Force = change in momentum ÷ time = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 N. This uses the impulse-momentum theorem: F = Δp/t.

questions.question: Why does a gun recoil backward when a bullet is fired forward?
options: The explosion pushes everything outward equally
Newton's Third Law — the gun and bullet exert equal and opposite forces on each other
The bullet is lighter so the gun moves more
questions.correct_answer: Newton's Third Law — the gun and bullet exert equal and opposite forces on each other
questions.explanation: The gun pushes the bullet forward; the bullet pushes the gun backward with equal force. Conservation of momentum also explains this: total momentum stays zero.

questions.question: A car decelerates from 25 m/s to 5 m/s in 4 seconds. What is the deceleration?
questions.explanation: a = (v − u)/t = (5 − 25)/4 = −20/4 = −5 m/s². The deceleration magnitude is 5 m/s².

questions.question: What force is needed to give a 2000 kg car an acceleration of 0.5 m/s²?
A car and a motorcycle collide. Which experiences the greater force of impact?
questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law: action and reaction forces are always equal in magnitude. The car and motorcycle exert equal forces on each other — the difference is in their resulting accelerations.

questions.question: A 10 kg object is on a surface with μ = 0.5. A 60 N force is applied. What is the net force? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Friction = μmg = 0.5 × 10 × 10 = 50 N. Net force = Applied − Friction = 60 − 50 = 10 N.

questions.question: An object moves at constant 12 m/s. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means no change in speed or direction. Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time = 0 ÷ t = 0 m/s².

questions.question: A 500 g ball (0.5 kg) hits a wall at 10 m/s and bounces back at 10 m/s. What is the change in momentum?
questions.explanation: Change in momentum = m(v₂ − v₁) = 0.5 × (10 − (−10)) = 0.5 × 20 = 10 kg·m/s. Direction reverses so velocities have opposite signs.

questions.question: Two objects have the same momentum. Object A has greater mass than Object B. Which has greater velocity?
questions.explanation: p = mv. If p is the same for both but A has greater mass, then A must have smaller velocity. B has smaller mass so it must have greater velocity.

questions.question: A 3 kg object at rest is pushed with 12 N. Friction is 3 N. What is the acceleration?
questions.explanation: Net force = 12 − 3 = 9 N. a = F/m = 9 ÷ 3 = 3 m/s².

questions.question: What mass would accelerate at 6 m/s² under a net force of 42 N?
A ball of mass 2 kg falls freely from rest for 3 seconds. What is its velocity just before hitting the ground? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: v = u + at = 0 + 10 × 3 = 30 m/s. In free fall, acceleration equals g.

questions.question: Why does doubling speed have more impact on stopping distance than doubling mass?
options: Speed affects friction more than mass does
Kinetic energy depends on v², so doubling speed quadruples it
Mass does not affect stopping distance at all
Speed increases momentum while mass decreases it
questions.correct_answer: Kinetic energy depends on v², so doubling speed quadruples it
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv². If v doubles, KE quadruples. If m doubles, KE only doubles. Stopping distance is proportional to kinetic energy, so speed has a greater impact.

questions.question: A 12 N force acts on a 4 kg object for 5 seconds. What is the change in momentum?
questions.explanation: Impulse = Force × time = 12 × 5 = 60 N·s = 60 kg·m/s. Impulse equals change in momentum.

questions.question: An object decelerates from 20 m/s to rest under friction of 10 N. If mass is 5 kg, how long does it take to stop?
A boat moves forward when oars push water backward. Which law explains this?
questions.explanation: The oars exert a backward force on water (action); water exerts an equal forward force on the boat (reaction). Newton's Third Law pairs always act on different objects.

questions.question: A 20 kg crate is pushed with 80 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. What is the net force? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Friction = μmg = 0.2 × 20 × 10 = 40 N. Net force = 80 − 40 = 40 N.

questions.question: What is the acceleration of the 20 kg crate in the previous question?
questions.explanation: a = F_net/m = 40 ÷ 20 = 2 m/s².

questions.question: A heavier and lighter car brake with the same force. Which stops in a shorter distance?
options: Both stop in the same distance
questions.explanation: Same braking force on a lighter car gives it greater deceleration (a = F/m). Greater deceleration means shorter stopping distance at the same initial speed.

questions.question: A 7 kg object accelerates at 4 m/s². What net force acts on it?
A 1500 kg car brakes from 30 m/s to rest in 10 s. What braking force is applied?
Why do we bend our knees when landing after a jump?
options: To extend the time of impact and reduce the force
questions.correct_answer: To extend the time of impact and reduce the force
questions.explanation: F = Δp/t. If the same momentum change occurs over a longer time (bent knees), the force is smaller. This is why airbags, cushioned shoes, and crash mats all work.

questions.question: An object of mass 9 kg has a momentum of 45 kg·m/s. What is its velocity?
A 6 kg object moves at 4 m/s. A 2 N friction force acts on it. How long before it stops?
If a net force acts on an object at right angles to its velocity, what happens?
options: The object changes direction without changing speed
questions.correct_answer: The object changes direction without changing speed
questions.explanation: A force perpendicular to velocity changes direction but not speed — like circular motion. The force affects direction, not the magnitude of velocity.

questions.question: Two forces act on an object: 30 N rightward and 18 N leftward. Mass is 4 kg. What is the acceleration?
questions.explanation: Net force = 30 − 18 = 12 N rightward. a = F/m = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 m/s² rightward.

questions.question: A 0.1 kg bullet is fired at 400 m/s from a 2 kg gun. What is the recoil velocity of the gun?
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum: 0 = m_b × v_b + m_g × v_g → 0 = 0.1×400 + 2×v_g → v_g = −40/2 = −20 m/s. Recoil speed is 20 m/s.

questions.question: When is friction a useful force rather than a nuisance?
options: When sliding boxes across a floor
When braking a vehicle or gripping a surface
When an object falls through air
questions.correct_answer: When braking a vehicle or gripping a surface
questions.explanation: Friction is essential for braking, walking, gripping, and writing. Without it, wheels would spin and we couldn't stop or start moving.

questions.question: A 500 kg elevator accelerates upward at 2 m/s². What is the tension in the cable? (g = 10 m/s²)
What is the weight of a 25 kg object on Earth? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Weight = mg = 25 × 10 = 250 N.

questions.question: Why does a parachute help slow a skydiver's fall?
options: It increases air resistance, reducing net downward force
It removes gravity from the skydiver
questions.correct_answer: It increases air resistance, reducing net downward force
questions.explanation: The parachute increases drag (air resistance). This upward force partially balances gravity, reducing net downward force and therefore deceleration.

questions.question: A 3 kg object is dropped from rest. What is its momentum after 4 seconds? (g = 10 m/s²)
A 10 kg trolley moving at 6 m/s collides with a stationary 5 kg trolley and they move together. What is the final velocity?
questions.explanation: p_initial = 10×6 = 60 kg·m/s. p_final = (10+5)×v → v = 60/15 = 4 m/s.

questions.question: An object's velocity changes from 5 m/s east to 5 m/s west. Has its momentum changed?
options: No — the speed is the same
Yes — direction has reversed so momentum has changed
Only if a force acted on it
Momentum cannot change without changing mass
questions.correct_answer: Yes — direction has reversed so momentum has changed
questions.explanation: Momentum is a vector. Changing direction changes momentum even if speed stays the same. Change in momentum = m×(−5) − m×(5) = −10m.

questions.question: A 4 kg block accelerates at 3 m/s². Friction is 4 N. What applied force is needed?
questions.explanation: F_net = ma = 4 × 3 = 12 N. Applied force = F_net + friction = 12 + 4 = 16 N.

questions.question: In a collision, why does the lighter vehicle suffer more damage than the heavier one?
options: The same force causes greater acceleration in the lighter vehicle
It moves faster after the collision
questions.correct_answer: The same force causes greater acceleration in the lighter vehicle
questions.explanation: From a = F/m: the same impact force produces greater acceleration (and deceleration) on the lighter vehicle, causing more structural damage.

questions.question: A 2 kg object moving at 10 m/s is brought to rest by a constant force in 0.5 seconds. What is the magnitude of the force?
